reference: GNU coreutils date, executed by the harness in reference mode with the same Bash fixture, C locale, and UTC baseline. Each parity case compares the reference status, stdout bytes, stderr policy, and resulting fixture tree against the candidate. The type/help contract case uses documented Bash builtin metadata and the loadable help registration as its independent expectation.
coverage: Default output plus signed epoch seconds and explicit UTC/offset ISO timestamps
Fractional epoch timestamps, including negative and sub-nanosecond values, with GNU %N widths
Local parsing and formatting under a deterministic POSIX timezone rule
GNU ISO-8601, RFC 3339, RFC email, and extended strftime formats
Documented compact, slash-separated, and RFC-style date input shapes
Invalid calendar input statuses and invalid ISO timespec status
Bash type/help metadata for the registered date builtin
-r/--reference=FILE modification times and their conflicts with -d (guest compatibility pass 1).

Guest pass 4 G57: a TZ="ZONE" prefix in -d strings (escapes, spacing, with relative items and @SECONDS), zone-plus-offset items (UTC+3, UTC-0500, UTC+05:30, EST+1, out of range), and 'extra operand' for a second operand.
Pass 8 (G120): option errors in GNU form, naming the command only, with the GNU status.
exclusions: Current-time output and the documented now input alias are omitted because they depend on wall-clock timing.
Natural-language date arithmetic and GNU options outside the documented loadable interface are not covered.
Setting the system wall clock is deferred; it would mutate clock state and requires a disposable VM or a reviewed clock syscall mock.

cases.purpose: Compare the default output format, signed epoch seconds, Z timestamps, and an explicit +05:30 offset after UTC conversion.
Compare GNU fractional epoch normalization before and after the epoch, including values with more than nine fractional digits, using full and truncated nanosecond formats.
Check local-time interpretation, daylight/standard offset selection, and conversion of an explicit UTC timestamp using a fixed POSIX timezone rule.
Compare epoch, nanosecond precision, colonized UTC offsets, 12/24-hour padding, lowercase meridian, and case-folded weekday formats.
Compare date-only, hours, minutes, and seconds ISO-8601 output plus RFC 3339 and RFC email output for a fixed offset timestamp.
cases.script:
stamp='2024-02-29T12:34:56+05:30'
date -d "$stamp" -I
date -d "$stamp" -Ihours
date -d "$stamp" --iso-8601=minutes
date -d "$stamp" --iso-8601=seconds
date -d "$stamp" --rfc-3339=date
date -d "$stamp" --rfc-3339=seconds
date -d "$stamp" -R

cases.purpose: Compare compact YYYYMMDD, slash-separated date-time, and RFC-style email timestamp parsing against GNU date.
Verify GNU-compatible failure status for invalid Gregorian dates while capturing each diagnostic inside command substitution so wording differences do not obscure the status comparison.
cases.script:
for value in '2024-02-30' '2023-02-29' '2024-04-31T12:00:00Z' '30 Feb 2024 00:00:00 UTC'; do
  rc=0
  diagnostic=$(date -u -d "$value" +%F 2>&1) || rc=$?
  printf '%s:%s\n' "$value" "$rc"
done

cases.purpose: Check GNU date's exit status for an invalid ISO-8601 timespec. Preserve a candidate status difference as a failure.
Confirm Bash reports date as a builtin and exposes its registered help text; this is metadata coverage, not operation coverage.
cases.script:
kind=$(type -t date)
[[ $kind == builtin ]]
help date >/dev/null
printf '%s\n' "$kind" 'help available'

cases.purpose: GNU date can request a system wall-clock change, but exercising that operation here would mutate clock state and the loadable documentation does not advertise it.
cases.reason: Do not execute date -s or another clock-setting path in this environment. A future test requires a disposable VM with an isolated controllable wall clock, or a reviewed clock syscall mock that records the requested timestamp without changing the host clock.

cases.purpose: -r FILE, -rFILE and --reference=FILE print FILE's modification time (guest pass 1, G14).
cases.script:
touch -d @1234567890 f
date -u -r f +%s
date -u -rf '+%F %T'
date -u --reference=f +%s
date -u -r f -d now +%s || echo rc=$?
date -r missing || echo rc=$?

cases.purpose: GNU date -d calendar items: month names in either order, MM/DD/YYYY, D-Mon-YYYY, the default date(1) output read back, fractional seconds, am/pm, zone abbreviations and numeric zones, YYYYMMDD HHMM, and relative items after such a date (guest pass 2, G29).
Strings GNU date rejects stay rejected with status 1: a month without its day, an out-of-range day or month, an ordinal suffix, a two-digit hour-like year without a comma (guest pass 2, G29).
cases.script:
export TZ=UTC0
for s in 'Mar' 'Mar 2024' 'Mar 32 2024' '13/05/2024' 'Feb 29 2023' 'march 5th 2024' 'Mar 5 24' '2024-03-05 25:00' '13pm'; do
  date -d "$s" +%F || echo "rc=$? $s"
done

cases.purpose: -f FILE, --file=FILE and -f - parse one date per line; a bad line is diagnosed and the rest still print with status 1; -f conflicts with -d and a missing file fails (guest pass 2, G29).
cases.script:
printf '2024-03-05
bogus
Mar 6 2024
@0
' > dates
date -u -f dates +%F || echo rc=$?
printf '2024-03-07
5 Mar 2024 10:00
' | date -u -f - '+%F %T'
date -u --file=dates -d now || echo rc=$?
date -u -f missing || echo rc=$?

cases.purpose: +%q quarter (with GNU padding flags), -Ins, --iso-8601=ns, --rfc-3339=ns and argmatch abbreviations such as -Is and --rfc-3339=s (guest pass 2, G29).
GNU tools answer --help with help on stdout and status 0; date --help used to write usage to stderr or exit nonzero (guest pass 2, G38).
cases.script: date --help >o 2>e; echo rc=$?; [[ -s o && ! -s e ]] && echo stdout-only

cases.purpose: G57: TZ="ZONE" before a date string reads the rest in ZONE (POSIX TZ rules), output staying in the process zone; leading blanks, no blank after the quote, \" escapes, relative items, @SECONDS and an empty rest (midnight in ZONE) work as in GNU; lower-case tz= is not the prefix.
G57: tz="..." in lower case and an unterminated TZ=" are invalid dates (exit 1).
cases.script:
date -d 'tz="UTC+5" 2024-01-01' || echo rc=$?
date -d 'TZ="UTC+5 2024-01-01' || echo rc=$?

cases.purpose: G57: reading a TZ="ZONE" date string does not change the TZ variable or the environment, whether TZ is unset, a shell variable, exported, or an assignment in front of date.
cases.script:
unset TZ
date -d 'TZ="UTC+5" 2024-01-01' +%s
declare -p TZ 2>/dev/null || echo unset
TZ=UTC-9
date -d 'TZ="UTC+5" 2024-01-01' +%s
declare -p TZ
export TZ=UTC-2
date -d 'TZ="UTC+5" 2024-01-01' +%s
declare -p TZ
date -d @0 +%H
TZ=UTC-3 date -d 'TZ="UTC+5" 2024-01-01 00:00' '+%s %H'
declare -p TZ
date -d @0 +%H
f() { local TZ=UTC-4; date -d 'TZ="UTC+5" 2024-01-01' +%s; declare -p TZ; date -d @0 +%H; }
f
declare -p TZ

cases.purpose: G57: a zone followed by an offset (parse-datetime's 'zone: tZONE tSNUMBER o_colon_minutes'): one or two digits are hours, three or four HHMM, H:MM with a colon; the offset adds to the zone (EST+1 is UTC-4); a signed number followed by a unit is a relative item instead; more than 24 hours is invalid.
G57: UTC+25 is not a valid zone offset (exit 1).
G57: two +FORMAT operands are an error, exactly as GNU words it, with exit 1.
G57: a +FORMAT after the POSIX set form, and one after -d, are extra operands too (exit 1).
cases.script:
date -d @0 +%F +%T || echo rc=$?
date -u 0101 +%F || echo rc=$?
date -u +%F -- +%T || echo rc=$?

cases.purpose: G120: an unknown long option is reported as date reports it, with no internal builtin name and the GNU status.
G120: an unknown short option is reported as date reports it, with no internal builtin name and the GNU status.
G120: -d without its argument.
Docker parity numbers/date-hash-flag: %#X is GNU's opposite case: uppercase names for %a %A %b %B %h, lowercase %p and %Z ("utc" under -u); %P stays lowercase under ^ and #.
